How is the LRU page replacement algorithm implemented in software, and what is its trade-off?
reference_answer: The OS maintains a list of pages ordered by the time of their last access. Upon a page access, the page is moved to the front of the list. The victim page is the one at the end of the list. The trade-off is that it is slow upon every memory access but fast upon replacement.

question: How is a cache access performed in a direct-mapped cache and in a fully-associative cache?
reference_answer: In a direct-mapped cache: 1a. Compare Tag[Index(A)] with Tag(A). If equal, it is a cache hit and data is read from Data[Index(A)]. If not equal, it is a cache miss, data is fetched from main memory, and the tag and data are inserted at address Index(A). 1b. Select the addressed part of the memory block based on Block-Offset(A). In a fully-associative cache: 1a. Check if there exists an i such that Tag[i] equals Tag(A). If yes, it is a cache hit and data is read from Data[i]. If for all i Tag[i] ≠ Tag(A), it is a cache miss, data is fetched from main memory, and the tag and data are inserted according to a replacement policy. 1b. Select the addressed part of the memory block based on Block-Offset(A).
